**June 23, 1956 — a Saturday**

The summer you were born into felt, to many people, like the Cold War might be thawing. Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin four months earlier had suggested the Soviet system might be capable of reform. Eisenhower and his Dulles-era brinkmanship seemed to be producing something like stability. After a decade of perpetual crisis — the Marshall Plan, Korea, the hydrogen bomb — 1956 looked briefly like it might be quieter.

It wasn't.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, Egypt ratified a new constitution in a national plebiscite that simultaneously confirmed Gamal Abdel Nasser as President. It was not a close vote. Nasser had already spent two years consolidating power after the 1952 revolution; this was the formal consecration. He emerged from it with a mandate and a plan. Thirty-three days later, on July 26, he nationalized the Suez Canal Company. Britain and France — its principal shareholders, and the powers most invested in keeping the canal under Western control — were furious. By October, Israel had invaded Egypt, followed by British and French forces. The United States refused to support them, the operation collapsed in humiliation, and the era of British and French authority in the Middle East effectively ended. Nasser became the most celebrated figure in the Arab world.

That sequence — nationalization, war, and Western humiliation — traces directly from the plebiscite on the day you were born.

---

**Five days after your birth**, on June 28, workers in Poznań, Poland took to the streets. They were protesting wages and working conditions in one of the country's largest industrial facilities. Soviet forces and Polish security services suppressed the uprising. At least 53 people were killed, hundreds wounded. The Poznań riots were the first significant workers' revolt against Communist rule in Eastern Europe — a direct tremor from Khrushchev's secret speech, which had delegitimized the Stalinist framework without providing anything to replace it. The Eastern bloc was not thawing. It was cracking. Four months later, Hungary erupted.

**Six days after your birth**, on June 29, President Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act, authorizing the Interstate Highway System. Forty-one thousand miles. The largest public works project in American history. You entered a country without interstates; by the time you finished elementary school, the system was already reshaping where Americans lived and how they moved.

Also on June 29: Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe married. The playwright and the film star. It lasted four years and became one of the defining celebrity relationships of the era. A footnote, perhaps, but the week of your birth was not a quiet one.

---

**The Montgomery Bus Boycott** was in its seventh month. Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat in December 1955; the Black community of Montgomery was still walking, still organized, still holding. The legal case was working through the courts. The boycott would succeed in December 1956, and the movement's architecture — its discipline, its legal strategy, its young minister — would sustain the next decade of struggle.

**Rock and roll** was at its precise moment of breakthrough. "Heartbreak Hotel" had reached number one in April. Three weeks after your birth, on July 13, Elvis Presley would release "Hound Dog" and "Don't Be Cruel" as a double A-side single — the record that made the argument definitively. You were born into the last days before Elvis was inescapable.

---

**Seventy years.**

You were born in the last year a reasonable person could have believed the British Empire retained its old authority — the Suez Crisis ended that. You grew up with the civil rights movement and rock and roll as the ambient conditions of childhood. You were a teenager when Kennedy was killed, twenty when the Bicentennial happened, thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell. The Soviet empire that Khrushchev was struggling to reform when you were born dissolved before you were forty.

The Nasser who was confirmed as President on your birthday outlasted the British empire in the Middle East, outlasted three wars, and died in 1970. The Interstate Highway System that was authorized the week you were born is now showing its age. The rock and roll that was in its first season when you arrived has been through fifty years of reinvention and is still here.

You entered a world that thought it was settling into a new order. It was doing no such thing.
